common_name: Winecraft Gold Smokebush (Compact Chartreuse-Gold Foliage Smoke Tree)
directions: Plant in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun for the brightest, longest-lasting color. Winecraft Gold is a compact selection of smokebush with rounded chartreuse-gold leaves that hold their color through summer heat better than older gold-leaf types, backed by the same airy, smoke-like pink flower plumes typical of the species. Its dense, rounded habit fits easily into mixed borders where a taller species-type smoke tree would be out of scale, and the foliage turns shades of orange and red before dropping in fall. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor rocky soils once established, and benefits from an occasional thinning of old wood in late winter to keep the shape tidy.

common_name: Young Lady Smokebush (Free-Flowering Compact Smoke Tree)
directions: Plant in average, well-drained, even lean soil in full sun; Young Lady tolerates dry, rocky sites where richer soil would encourage floppy growth and dull flowering. This compact green-leaved smokebush selection is valued for blooming heavily and reliably even as a young plant, producing dense, smoky-pink flower panicles in early summer that persist for weeks as they age to a soft tan. Fall color shifts to yellow, orange, and reddish-purple tones before leaf drop. Prune out a few of the oldest stems in late winter every year or two to keep the rounded form open and encourage strong new flowering wood.

common_name: Notcutt's Variety Smokebush (Deep Purple Vigorous Smoke Tree)
directions: Plant in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun for the deepest foliage color; part shade fades the purple tone toward green. One of the oldest and most vigorous purple-leaf smokebush cultivars, Notcutt's Variety grows larger and more tree-like than newer compact selections, with rich wine-purple foliage all season and abundant smoky pink-purple flower plumes in summer. Fall color develops into striking scarlet and orange tones. Because of its size, give it room in the back of a border or use it as a specimen; renewal-prune a portion of old stems each late winter to maintain vigor and shape rather than shearing the whole plant.

common_name: Flame Smoketree (Large Orange-Red Fall Color Smoke Tree)
directions: Plant container-grown stock in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Flame grows larger and more tree-like than most purple-leaf smokebush cultivars and needs room to reach its mature size. It carries green-to-blue-green summer foliage rather than the purple tones of coggygria selections, but is prized above all for an exceptional fall display of brilliant orange, scarlet, and red that ranks among the best of any smoke tree. Airy, smoke-like flower panicles appear in early summer on established plants. It is tolerant of heat, drought, and poor soils once rooted in, and needs only occasional removal of crossing or crowded branches in late winter to keep an open, small-tree form.

common_name: Orange Rocket Barberry (Narrow Columnar Orange-to-Burgundy Foliage Barberry)
directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; foliage color is most vivid with several hours of direct sun daily. Orange Rocket is a narrow, upright, columnar barberry whose new spring growth emerges bright orange-red before maturing to deep burgundy through summer, then flaring to vivid scarlet in fall, giving strong season-long color in a very slim footprint. Its tight vertical habit suits narrow borders, foundation plantings, and repeated accents along a walkway without the width of older barberry cultivars. It is drought-tolerant once established and needs no regular pruning to maintain form; note that Berberis thunbergii is restricted or banned as invasive in several US states, so check local regulations before planting.

Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, where the darkest foliage color develops; shade fades the color toward green-purple. Concorde is a very compact, tightly mounded barberry with some of the darkest foliage available in the group, emerging deep reddish-purple and maturing to nearly black-purple through the growing season. Its small, dense form makes it useful for low edging, rock gardens, and mass plantings where a low color accent is needed without the spread of larger barberry cultivars. It tolerates heat, drought, and poor soils once established and needs little to no pruning; Berberis thunbergii is restricted or banned as invasive in several US states, so check local regulations before planting.

Plant in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, with some afternoon shade in hotter climates. Native to Chile and Argentina, Darwin's barberry is an evergreen shrub with small, glossy, holly-like leaflets and a profuse spring display of small, deep orange flowers in drooping clusters, followed by edible blue-black berries that attract birds. It forms a dense, rounded, thorny mass useful as a barrier hedge or specimen in mild-winter climates such as the Pacific Northwest and coastal California, but it is not reliably hardy in colder inland regions. Once established it tolerates drought reasonably well, though it performs best with regular moisture; note it has naturalized and become invasive in parts of the Pacific Northwest and should be sited and monitored with that in mind.

common_name: Cutleaf Staghorn Sumac (Dissecta, Green Ferny-Leaved Sumac)
directions: Plant in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; this old cutleaf selection of staghorn sumac tolerates rocky, sandy, and dry sites where richer shrubs struggle. Its deeply dissected, fern-like green leaflets give the whole plant a soft, lacy texture distinct from the coarser foliage of the species, and it grows noticeably larger over time than newer dwarf gold-leaf cutleaf sumacs. Fall color turns brilliant orange, red, and purple, and female plants carry the same upright crimson fruit clusters typical of staghorn sumac. It suckers to form colonies over time, so give it room to naturalize or remove root suckers each season to keep it contained.

common_name: Cutleaf Smooth Sumac (Laciniata, Ferny-Leaved Smooth Sumac)
directions: Plant in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; smooth sumac and its cutleaf form thrive in lean, dry, rocky ground where few other shrubs perform well. This heirloom selection of smooth sumac carries finely dissected, fern-like leaflets that give it a delicate, airy texture compared with the straight species, while retaining the same upright reddish fruit spikes on female plants and vivid scarlet-orange fall color. It is a smaller, more refined-looking plant than staghorn sumac and lacks the fuzzy stems of that species, but still spreads by root suckers to form colonies, so plan to remove unwanted suckers or give it an area where naturalizing is welcome.
